# Sensing and Perception {#sec-sensing}

Navigation estimates where a system is, how it moves, and how it is oriented.
Perception supplies the physical evidence for that estimate. The two directions
belong together: a state estimate predicts what a sensor should observe, and an
observation tests whether the state estimate is plausible.

## A Sensor Is Not a State Estimate {#sec-sensing-sensor-not-state}

It is tempting to say that a GNSS receiver “gives position” or an IMU “gives
attitude.” What each device actually provides is a measurement with a frame,
timestamp, uncertainty, and failure modes. The estimator supplies the model that
relates that measurement to the state:

$$
\mathbf{z}_k = h(\mathbf{x}_k) + \mathbf{v}_k.
$$

The function $h$ predicts the measurement; $\mathbf{v}_k$ describes the part the
model does not explain. A good measurement interface records at least:

- the time at which the quantity was valid, not only arrival time;
- units and the frame in which its components are expressed;
- a covariance, accuracy estimate, or quality indicator;
- calibration and extrinsic information needed by $h$; and
- validity, saturation, tracking, or fault flags.

This contract is what makes a camera observation, lidar range, GNSS solution, and
magnetometer reading usable by the same estimation machinery.

## Proprioception and Exteroception {#sec-sensing-proprioception-exteroception}

Two broad sensor classes make the division of work clear:

| Class | Typical sensors | Navigation role | Common failure pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Proprioceptive | IMU, wheel encoder, airspeed, DVL | High-rate propagation | Bias and noise accumulate into drift |
| Exteroceptive | Camera, lidar, radar, sonar, GNSS, landmark detector | Measurement update or map constraint | Visibility, geometry, association, and outliers |

Neither class is sufficient everywhere. A vehicle can dead reckon smoothly for a
short time but drift over a long one. An external sensor can correct that drift but
may be obstructed, delayed, or fooled by a repeated-looking environment. Robust
navigation uses the different failure modes rather than pretending one sensor is
truth.

## From Hardware to an Estimator {#sec-sensing-from-hardware-estimator}

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sensor-measurement-contract
%%| fig-cap: "A measurement becomes useful only after its physical, timing, calibration, and uncertainty context is preserved."

flowchart LR
    A["Physical quantity"] --> B["Sensor and front end"]
    B --> C["Timestamped measurement"]
    C --> D["Calibration and frame adapter"]
    D --> E["Measurement model h(x), R, quality gates"]
    E --> F["Estimator update or rejection"]
```

The hardware front end may include filtering, synchronization, feature
extraction, or a receiver solution. Those operations can change latency and
correlation, so they belong in the measurement model rather than being treated as
invisible plumbing.

## What This Part Covers {#sec-sensing-what-this-part}

@sec-motion-models develops motion models and IMU measurements.
@sec-measurement-models turns physical observations into likelihoods;
@sec-feature-association addresses which feature generated an observation; and
@sec-pnp builds the camera observation model used in Module 1. The
global-navigation chapters (@sec-global-nav onward) return to this contract for GNSS, where signal quality and time validity matter just as
much as position.
